title: Katakana T-Row — タ チ ツ テ ト

points.name: タ
points.explanation: タ makes the same 'ta' sound as hiragana た (unaspirated 't' + 'ah'). Visually, タ looks like it could be related to the Roman letter 'T' — it has two strokes: a near-horizontal stroke going slightly down-right, then a diagonal sweeping to the lower right from near its center. Compare to サ (sa), which has three strokes; タ is a slightly simpler two-stroke character. Memory trick: タ looks like the front of a taxi seen from above, or like the letter 'T' with a diagonal added. タ appears in タクシー (taxi), タオル (towel), and タブレット (tablet).
rules: タ has two strokes — a near-horizontal, then a sweeping diagonal from its center.
Memory: タ looks like 'T' with a diagonal added — 'T' for 'ta'.

points.name: チ
points.explanation: チ makes the same 'chi' sound as hiragana ち — always 'chi', never 'ti'. Visually, チ resembles the Roman numeral 'III' with a long bottom stroke, or a stylized letter 'F' facing right. It has three strokes: two short horizontals at the top, then a longer sweeping stroke curving to the lower right. Compare this to hiragana ち, which has a more complex looping structure. チ appears in チョコレート (chocolate — チョ is a combination), チーム (team), and チケット (ticket).
rules: Always 'chi', never 'ti' — same irregularity as hiragana ち.
チ has three strokes: two short horizontals + a long sweeping curve.
チョコレート (chocolate) uses the チョ combination — チ + small ョ = 'cho'.
points.flashcardAnswer: chi — same sound as ち (always 'chi', not 'ti')

points.name: ツ
points.explanation: ツ makes the same 'tsu' sound as hiragana つ. As noted with シ, ツ is famously confused with シ (shi) by beginners. The definitive rule: ツ's two short strokes lean to the LEFT (pointing back), while シ's lean to the RIGHT. Think of ツ as a sneeze (tsu!) — the strokes blast LEFT. ツ appears in ツアー (tour), ツール (tool), and ツナ (tuna). The small version ッ (double consonant marker) is one of the most commonly used elements in katakana loanwords — you'll see it in words like チケット (ticket), コーヒー, etc.
rules: Always 'tsu' as in 'tsunami' — same irregularity as hiragana つ.
ツ vs シ: ツ's short strokes lean LEFT; シ's lean RIGHT. Crucial distinction!
Small ッ marks a doubled consonant: チケット (chi-ke-t-to), ベッド (be-d-do).

examples.english: beach (notice ツ in ツ-related context)

points.flashcardAnswer: tsu — same sound as つ; strokes lean LEFT (opposite of シ)

points.name: テ
points.explanation: テ makes the same 'te' sound as hiragana て. Visually, テ is one of the most elegant katakana characters — it looks like a capital Roman letter 'T' with an extra horizontal stroke, or like three stacked horizontal strokes with a vertical. Some describe it as an 'umbrella stand' shape. テ appears constantly in modern vocabulary: テレビ (television), テスト (test), テーブル (table), and テーマ (theme). These words alone make テ immediately essential for navigating modern Japanese life.
rules: Same 'te' as て — unaspirated 't' + pure 'eh' vowel.
テ looks like a capital 'T' with an extra horizontal stroke, or a three-bar horizontal shape.
テレビ (TV) and テスト (test) are words you'll use constantly in school and daily life contexts.
points.flashcardAnswer: te — same sound as て; looks like a capital 'T' with extra stroke

points.name: ト
points.explanation: ト makes the same 'to' sound as hiragana と. Visually, ト is beautifully simple — just two strokes: a vertical line with a short horizontal tick pointing to the right, near its middle. It looks exactly like a door or a cross with the bottom removed — which is why many learners use the phrase 'ト = two strokes for to' as a memory hook. ト appears in トイレ (toilet / restroom — one of the most important words for any traveler!), トマト (tomato), and トースト (toast). Knowing how to ask for トイレはどこですか? (Where is the restroom?) is practically survival Japanese.
rules: ト is two simple strokes: a vertical with a tick sticking right. Very easy to write!
トイレはどこですか? (Where is the restroom?) — one of the most important phrases to learn early.
points.flashcardAnswer: to — same sound as と; looks like a vertical line with a tick

chapterPractice.prompt: ツ and シ look similar. What sound does ツ make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ツ makes the 'tsu' sound (like 'tsunami'). Remember: ツ's short strokes lean LEFT; シ's lean RIGHT. You can think of ツ as a sneeze: 'tsu!' blasting the strokes left.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana テ?
chapterPractice.explanation: テ and て both make the 'te' sound. テ looks like a capital 'T' with an extra horizontal stroke; て has a more flowing, cursive hook structure.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: テレビ (terebi) means 'television'. テ (te) + レ (re) + ビ (bi) = terebi. This comes from the English word 'television', shortened and adapted to Japanese phonology.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: トイレ (toire) means 'toilet' or 'restroom'. ト (to) + イ (i) + レ (re) = toire. This is essential vocabulary — トイレはどこですか? means 'Where is the restroom?'
